title: Catalysts that skip the wait
question: How can a cell run reactions in milliseconds that would otherwise take forever?
hook: One reaction in your cells would take millions of years on its own, yet it finishes in a blink.
idea: Enzymes lower the activation energy of a reaction, so it runs fast, and they come out of each cycle ready to go again.

beats.prompt: A reaction would otherwise take millions of years. The cell adds its enzyme, orotidine 5′-phosphate decarboxylase. About how long does it take now?

choices.label: Still thousands of years
choices.feedback: Enzymes speed reactions up by factors of millions, so thousands of years is far too slow.

choices.label: A few days
choices.feedback: That is a big speed-up, but this enzyme does far better than days.

beats.explain: This enzyme accelerates a reaction that would otherwise take millions of years so that it occurs in milliseconds.

beats.prompt: Put these moments in the story of enzymes in order.
items: Kühne first uses the word enzyme
Buchner submits his first paper on yeast extracts
The structure of lysozyme is published
beats.explain: Diastase was found in 1833, the word enzyme was first used in 1877, Buchner’s first paper came in 1897, and the lysozyme structure appeared in 1965.

beats.prompt: Match each enzyme to what it does.
pairs: Digests the coating of some bacteria
beats.explain: Enzymes are specific: each is named for, and suited to, the substrate or reaction it handles.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: An enzyme speeds up a reaction by lowering its activation energy.
The enzyme is regenerated at the end of each cycle, so it is not used up.
Because it pushes the reaction forward, it also moves the final balance toward more product.
So adding more enzyme would bring the reaction to its end point sooner, with the same balance.
beats.explain: Like all catalysts, enzymes do not affect the overall equilibrium of a reaction.
